column2: When the two winds, prana and apana, overpower each other, that is the twofold method; by restraining both there is a third.
For the yogi who practises it with a support, best of the twice-born, the gross form of the Infinite is declared to be the support.
The knower of yoga, devoted to pratyahara, should restrain the senses attached to sound and the other objects and make them follow the mind.
By this arises supreme mastery over the exceedingly restless senses; with them uncontrolled, the yogi cannot accomplish yoga.
Having brought the breaths under control by pranayama and the senses by pratyahara, one should then fix the mind on its auspicious support.
Tell me, fortunate one, what is the mind's auspicious support, resting on which it destroys all that springs from faults.
The support of the mind is Brahman, and in its nature it is twofold, O king: with form and formless, supreme and non-supreme.
Know, O king, that this universe has a threefold contemplation: that called Brahman, that called action, and that consisting of both.
One consists of the contemplation of action, another of the contemplation of Brahman, and another of both; thus the contemplation of being is threefold.
Sanandana and the others are endowed with the contemplation of Brahman; others, the gods and the rest, moving and unmoving, with the contemplation of action.
In Hiranyagarbha and the others, who are endowed with authority and awakening, the twofold contemplation consisting of Brahman and action exists.
As long as all the acts of particular knowledge are not exhausted, the universe appears as this and as something other and supreme to those whose vision is divided by difference, O king.
That knowledge in which difference has set, which is mere being, beyond the reach of words and known only to the self — that is called Brahman.
And that is the supreme form of the formless Vishnu, unborn and imperishable, marked by its unlikeness to the form of the universe, belonging to the supreme self.
Since that cannot be meditated on by one beginning yoga, O king, one should meditate on Hari's gross form, which the universe can perceive:
the blessed Hiranyagarbha, Vasava and Prajapati, the Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, suns, stars and planets,
gandharvas, yakshas, daityas and all the divine orders, men, beasts, mountains, oceans, rivers and trees,
all beings, O king, and the causes of beings, from pradhana down to the specific elements, conscious and unconscious,
one-footed, two-footed, many-footed and footless — this is Hari's form with shape, consisting of the three contemplations.

All this universe, this world of moving and unmoving, is pervaded by the power of Vishnu, whose nature is the supreme Brahman; and the manifestations of power from that reality are called the command of the all-pervading one.
Vishnu's power is declared supreme; another, called the knower of the field, is lower; and a third power, called ignorance or action, is recognized.
Enveloped by it, O king, the all-pervading power of the knower of the field undergoes all the unending torments of worldly existence.
And because it is concealed by that, the power called the knower of the field is seen in all beings in varying degree, lord of the earth:
very slight in lifeless things, more in the unmoving, more than them in reptiles, and in birds with still greater power;
more than birds in wild beasts, and more than them in domestic animals; and more than animals in men, empowered by the power of the spirit;
more than them the nagas, gandharvas, yakshas and the other divine beings, O king;
Shakra more than all the gods, and Prajapati more than him; and Hiranyagarbha more than him, marked by the power of the spirit.
All these forms are his forms, lord of the earth, since they are joined with his power as with space.
The second form of Brahman called Vishnu, to be meditated on by yogis, wise one, is formless, which the wise call "the Real."
That in which all these powers are established, O king, is another great form of Hari, of the form of the universe.
That form, lord of people, creates in its own play forms of all powers, active as gods, animals, men and the rest,
for the benefit of the worlds; that activity of the immeasurable one is not caused by karma; it is all-pervading and unobstructed.
That form of him who has the universe as his form, O king, is to be meditated on by the practitioner of yoga for the purification of the self; it destroys all sins.
As a fire with rising flames, fanned by the wind, burns dry grass, so Vishnu abiding in the mind burns all the sins of yogis.
Therefore one should fix the mind on that support of all powers; that is to be known as pure dharana.
He is the auspicious support of the all-pervading mind and of the self, beyond the three contemplations, for the liberation of yogis, O king.
But the other supports of the mind, tiger among men — the gods and the rest, all born of karma — are impure.
The form of the Blessed One with shape, free of all other supports — this is declared to be dharana, when the mind is held there.
And hear, lord of men, how that form of Hari with shape is to be meditated on; dharana is not possible without a support.
With a gracious, lovely face, eyes like lotus petals, fine cheeks and a broad, shining forehead,
with lovely ear ornaments placed at the ends of evenly set ears, a neck like a conch, and a broad chest marked with the Shrivatsa,
with a belly having three folds and a deep navel, Vishnu with eight long arms or with four,
with evenly set thighs and shanks, well-placed lotus feet and hands — one should meditate on him who is Brahman, clad in pure yellow garments,
adorned with a crown, lovely armlets, bracelets and the like,
bearing the Sharnga bow, conch, mace, sword, discus and rosary, with hands granting boons and fearlessness and adorned with rings — the yogi, absorbed in him, should meditate, collecting his mind,
until the dharana becomes firm right there, O king. When, whether walking, standing or doing any other act at will, it does not leave the mind, then one should consider it perfected.
Then the wise one should meditate on the form of the Blessed One without conch, mace, discus, Sharnga and the rest, tranquil, with a rosary.
When that dharana likewise becomes steady, one should then remember him without ornaments such as the crown and armlets.
Then the wise one should meditate on the god as a single limb, and after that become intent on the whole.
A single continuous flow of ideas of that form, free of desire for anything else — that is dhyana, accomplished by the first six limbs, O king.
The grasping by the mind of his very nature, free of imagination, accomplished through meditation — that is called samadhi.
Knowledge is what leads to the supreme Brahman to be attained, lord of the earth; and the self, all its contemplations exhausted, is what is to be led there.
The knower of the field is the agent, knowledge the instrument; having accomplished by it his work of liberation, it ceases, its purpose fulfilled.
Having attained the state of that being, he becomes undivided from the supreme self; his difference was made by ignorance.
When the ignorance that produces difference has been utterly destroyed, who will make the unreal difference between the self and Brahman?
Thus I have told you yoga, Khandikya, as you asked, both briefly and in detail; what else can I do for you?"

Now that the true nature of yoga has been told, everything has been done for me, since by your teaching all the impurity of my mind has been destroyed.
vishnupurana:125:98	And the word 'mine' that I have spoken is untrue, and cannot be spoken otherwise, lord of men, even by those who know what is to be known.
vishnupurana:125:99	'I' and 'mine' — this is ignorance, and ordinary dealing goes on by it; but the highest truth cannot be spoken of, it is not within the range of words.
vishnupurana:125:100	So go for your good; you have done everything for me, since you have taught the yoga that grants liberation, imperishable Keshidhvaja.
Honoured duly with worship by that Khandikya, King Keshidhvaja then came back to his city, brahmin.
Khandikya too, having made his son king, went to the forest for the perfection of yoga, his mind fixed on Govinda.
There, delighting in solitude and purified by the yamas and other qualities, the king attained dissolution in the stainless Brahman called Vishnu.
Keshidhvaja too, intent on exhausting his own karma for the sake of liberation, enjoyed the objects of sense and performed actions without seeking their fruit.
And by experiences that were not auspicious his sins were exhausted; stainless, he then attained perfection, whose fruit is the utter end of torment, brahmin.
This Purana, equal to the Veda, which I have told you — on hearing it the mass of sins arising from all faults perishes.
Creation, secondary creation, lineages, the Manvantaras and the whole history of the dynasties have been told to you here by me.
Here gods and daityas, gandharvas, serpents and rakshasas, yakshas, vidyadharas, siddhas and apsarases are described;
sages of cultivated self endowed with austerity are described, the four castes of men and men of distinguished conduct,
holy regions of the earth, holy rivers and oceans, most holy mountains and the deeds of the wise,
the dharmas of castes and the rest and the branches of the Veda in full, by hearing which one is at once freed from all sins.
The imperishable cause of the world's origin, continuance and destruction, who is all beings and the self of all, the blessed Hari, is described here —

he by the mere mention of whose name, even involuntarily, a man is at once freed from all sins as deer are scattered by a frightened lion. This, destroying sin, I heard from Vyasa, and I have told you all of it, in seven thousand verses.
The glorification of whose name with devotion is the unsurpassed dissolver of all sins, Maitreya, as fire is of metals.

The most fierce impurity of the Kali age, which brings men the torment of hell, has as its supreme destroyer the remembrance of Hari with devotion; there is nothing, brahmin, that need be sought elsewhere, since all dissolves at once when he is remembered even once.
By Hiranyagarbha, the king of the gods, Rudra, the Adityas, the Ashvins and the winds, by the fires, the Vasus, the Sadhyas, the Vishvedevas and the other gods,
by yakshas, rakshasas and serpents, by siddhas, daityas, gandharvas and danavas, by apsarases, by the stars and asterisms and all the planets,
by the seven sages, by the celestial abodes and their lords, by brahmins and other men, by domestic animals and wild beasts,
by reptiles and birds, by trees such as the palasha, by forests, mountains, oceans, rivers and netherworlds, with the earth and the rest,
together with sound and the other objects — the whole cosmic egg, brahmin, is to him as an atom to Meru, and it consists of him, best of the twice-born.
He who is all, all-knowing, of the nature of all yet without form, the blessed Vishnu, destroyer of sin, is praised here; that is auspicious, bringing welfare, unsurpassed in purity.
Whatever fruit one obtains by bathing at the conclusion of a horse sacrifice, one obtains all of it by hearing this, best of sages.
What a man who has fasted at Prayaga, Pushkara, Kurukshetra and Arbuda obtains, he obtains by hearing this.
The fruit one obtains by a year of well-offered agnihotra, full of great merit, brahmin, one obtains by hearing this once.
What one obtains by bathing in the water of the Yamuna on the bright twelfth of Jyeshtha and seeing Hari at Mathura — the supreme goal —
that fruit one fully obtains by reciting it with concentration; by hearing this Purana with reverence, one becomes of good fame, brahmin sage, his mind offered to Keshava.
A man who bathes in the water of the Yamuna, best of sages, fasting on the twelfth of the bright fortnight under Jyeshtha and Mula,
and duly worships Achyuta at Mathura with collected mind, obtains the undiminished fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Seeing the prosperity of others raised up by their own descendants, the fathers and grandfathers of others, it is said, spoke thus:

Will one born in our family, bathed in the water of the Kalindi, worship Govinda at Mathura while fasting,
vishnupurana:126:37	in the bright fortnight under Jyeshtha and Mula, so that we too may attain supreme prosperity, rescued by those born of our family?
vishnupurana:126:38	One born in the family of the blessed, having worshipped Janardana in the bright fortnight under Jyeshtha and Mula, will offer pindas in the Yamuna.
Having worshipped Krishna there at that time with collected mind and offered pindas to the ancestors, bathed in the water of the Yamuna,
whatever merit a man obtains in rescuing his forefathers, the devoted one obtains by hearing a chapter of this Purana.

This is the unsurpassed protection for those who fear worldly existence; it destroys bad dreams for men and removes all evils; it is the most auspicious of auspicious things and bestows sons and wealth.
This sage's teaching the lotus-born one told long ago to Ribhu; Ribhu told it to Priyavrata, and he told it to Bhaguri;
Bhaguri to Stambhamitra, he to Dadhicha, and he told it to Sarasvata; and Bhrigu received it from Sarasvata.
Bhrigu told it to Purukutsa, and he to Narmada; Narmada to the naga Dhritarashtra and to Apurana;
by those two it was told to Vasuki, king of the nagas, brahmin; Vasuki told it to Vatsa, and Vatsa to Ashvatara;
he told it to Kambala, and Kambala to Elapatra.
Then the sage Vedashiras, having reached Patala, obtained all of it, and he gave it to Pramati.
It was given by Pramati to the wise Jatukarna, and Jatukarna told it to other men of merit.
Through the boon granted by Pulastya it came to my memory too; and I have told it to you duly, Maitreya.
You too will tell it to Shinika at the end of the Kali age.
Whatever man hears this supreme secret, which destroys the impurity of the Kali age, is freed from all sins, brahmin.

Whoever hears this day after day has made praise to the ancestors, yakshas, men and all the immortals. Having heard this whole great Vaishnava Purana, brahmin, one should honour the reader there as equal to Vyasa, best of the twice-born, and give him gold, cows and a garment according to one's means; when the reader is honoured, brahmin, Keshava is honoured.
The most rare merit arising from the gift of a tawny cow one obtains by hearing ten chapters of this, no doubt.

The man who hears all this, keeping in his mind Achyuta — who is all, consisting of all, the support of all worlds, resting in himself, knowledge and the knowable, infinite, beginningless, the benefactor of all the immortals — obtains the undiminished fruit of the horse sacrifice; there is no doubt.

That in which, at the beginning, middle and end, is the Blessed One, guru of the moving and unmoving, Achyuta consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, lord of the beginning, middle and end of the whole world — the man who hears, recites or holds with devotion this supreme purifier obtains what exists nowhere else in all the worlds: Hari, the one sure attainment.

He on whom one's mind is fixed does not go to hell, for whom even heaven is an obstacle in meditating on him, compared with whom, for one whose mind is set on him, even Brahma's world is small; the imperishable one who, abiding in the heart, grants liberation to men of pure understanding — what wonder that sin is dissolved when Achyuta is glorified?

He whom the ritualists, knowers of sacrifice, ever worship with sacrifices as lord of sacrifice; he whom the knowers meditate on as consisting of Brahman, beyond the higher and the lower; attaining whom one is not born, does not die, does not grow or decline, who is neither non-existent nor existent but beyond — what else is to be heard than of Hari?

The all-pervading one who, bearing the form of the ancestors, eats the offerings to the ancestors duly offered, and as a god the offerings to the gods; the blessed one without beginning or end, called Svaha and Svadha; the Brahman, abode of all powers, in which the measures of the measurers do not reach their conclusion — that Hari, when he reaches the ear, destroys impurity.
He who has no end and no origin, who has no growth, free of change, who does not undergo decay, the undifferentiated reality — to him, the Supreme Person, the Lord, the praiseworthy, I bow.

He who, though one, enjoys the qualities in many ways, though pure appears impure through the divisions of forms, endowed with knowledge, maker of the glories of all principles — to that ever imperishable Person I bow.

To him who consists of the unity of knowledge, activity and restraint, skilled in granting experience to the spirit, whose self is the three gunas, the unmanifest, the cause of the arising of existence, the becoming of his own nature, ever unaging — I bow. Om, salutation to the blessed Vasudeva. Victory to you, lotus-eyed one; salutation to you, creator of the universe; salutation to you, Hrishikesha, great Person, first-born.

To him who consists of the arrangement of space, wind, fire, water and earth, able to bring to the spirit the objects of enjoyment such as sound, who helps the spirit through all the instruments, manifest, subtle and stainless — I always bow.
May the blessed Hari, whose many forms of the unborn, eternal one consist of prakriti and the supreme self, grant to all men that perfection which is free of birth, old age and the rest.
